lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Isn’t that Heracles? Yes. No one else, by Heracles. The bow, the club, the lion-skin, the size — Heracles entire. And yet he’s dead, son of Zeus and all? Tell me, Champion: are you a corpse? Because up on earth I used to sacrifice to you as a god.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: And rightly. Heracles himself is in heaven with the gods, married to fine-ankled Hebe. I am his image.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What are you saying? The image of a god? Is it possible for a man to be half god, and dead on the other half?

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Yes. He didn’t die. I did — his likeness.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I see. He handed you over to Pluto as a substitute, instead of himself. So you’re dead on his behalf.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Something like that.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Then how did Aeacus, precise man that he is, fail to spot that you weren’t him? How did he accept a counterfeit Heracles presented at the desk?

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Because I looked exactly like him.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: True. Exactly like him — so exactly you might be him. Mind you, it may be the other way round: you are Heracles, and the image is upstairs with the gods, married to Hebe.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You are insolent and you talk too much. If you don’t stop making jokes at my expense, you will shortly learn what kind of god I am the image of.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Yes, the bow is strung and handy. But what exactly am I still supposed to fear from you, now that I’m dead once for all? Still — tell me, by your own Heracles: when he was alive, were you with him then too, as his image? Or were you one person during life, and once you died you split, with one part flying off to the gods, and you, the image, naturally reporting here to Hades?

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: I shouldn’t answer a man who quibbles like this. Still, hear this much. Whatever in Heracles came from Amphitryon has died; I am all of that. What came from Zeus is in heaven with the gods.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Now I understand perfectly. You’re saying Alcmene gave birth to two Heracleses at the same time: one by Amphitryon, one by Zeus. So you were twins by the same mother all along, and nobody noticed.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: No, you fool. The same person was both.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: That is not easy to grasp: two composite Heracleses — unless you were a sort of centaur arrangement, man and god grown together into one unit.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Don’t you think everyone is put together that way, from two parts, soul and body? So what prevents the soul — the part from Zeus — from being in heaven, and the mortal part, me, from being among the dead?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: My excellent son of Amphitryon, that would be a fine answer if you were a body. But as it stands you’re a bodiless image. You’re in danger of making Heracles triple.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Triple how?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Like this. If one Heracles is in heaven, and another is here with us — you, the image — and the body has dissolved and is now dust, that makes three. And you’d better think up a father for the third one, the body.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You’re insolent, and a sophist. Who are you, anyway?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: The image of Diogenes of Sinope. But Diogenes himself, by Zeus, is not among the immortal gods; he is here with the best of the dead, laughing at Homer and all this theological cold porridge.
